name: Grand Designs
subject: Architecture and famous buildings
tagline: Twenty questions on towers, temples, domes and the people who dreamed them up. Starts easy, ends hard.

questions.q: The Eiffel Tower was built as the entrance to which event?
o: The opening of the Paris Métro
questions.w: The 1889 Exposition Universelle, held for the centenary of the French Revolution.
questions.more: It was meant to stand for twenty years and be dismantled. Gustave Eiffel saved it by making it useful: a radio antenna on top sent signals that helped jam German communications in the First World War. It was the tallest structure in the world until the Chrysler Building in 1930.

questions.q: Which city is home to the Sagrada Família, the basilica under construction since 1882?
questions.w: Barcelona, where Antoni Gaudí took over the project in 1883 and worked on it until he died.
questions.more: Gaudí was hit by a tram in 1926 and, dressed shabbily, was taken for a beggar; he died in a pauper's ward. Work slowed for decades and his plaster models were smashed in the Civil War. The main tower is due to be finished for the centenary of his death in 2026.

questions.q: Which American city is home to the Willis Tower, better known by its old name, the Sears Tower?
questions.w: Chicago. It was the tallest building in the world from 1973 to 1998.
questions.more: Sears moved out in the early 1990s and the naming rights went to the insurance broker Willis in 2009, though many Chicagoans refuse to use the new name. Its design bundles nine square tubes of different heights, an idea its engineer said came from a pack of cigarettes.

questions.q: The Burj Khalifa, the tallest building in the world, stands in which city?
questions.w: Dubai. It opened in 2010 at 828 metres, more than twice the height of the Empire State Building.
questions.more: It was to be called the Burj Dubai, but was renamed at the opening in honour of the ruler of Abu Dhabi, whose emirate had bailed Dubai out during the 2009 debt crisis. From the top you can watch the sun set, take the lift down, and watch it set again.

questions.q: The famous leaning bell tower is in which Italian city?
questions.w: Pisa. It began to tilt during construction in the 1170s because of soft ground on one side.
questions.more: Builders tried to correct the lean by making the upper floors taller on the low side, which is why the tower is slightly banana-shaped. By 1990 it leaned 5.5 degrees and was closed; engineers removed soil from under the high side and pulled it back to about 4 degrees.

questions.q: The Empire State Building in New York is a famous example of which architectural style?
questions.w: Art Deco, with its stepped setbacks and stainless-steel spire.
questions.more: It went up in just 410 days during the Depression and opened in 1931 so empty that New Yorkers called it the Empty State Building. The mast on top was sold as a mooring post for airships, an idea abandoned after one terrifying attempt in high winds.

questions.q: True or false: the White House was first painted white to hide the scorch marks left when British troops burned it in 1814.
questions.w: False. It was whitewashed in 1798, before it was even finished, to protect the porous sandstone from frost.
questions.more: The name 'White House' was in use by the early 1800s, well before the fire, though it only became official when Theodore Roosevelt put it on the stationery in 1901. Repainting the outside today takes about 570 gallons of paint.

questions.q: Which architect designed the Sydney Opera House?
questions.w: Jørn Utzon, a Dane who won the 1957 competition with a sketch the judges had first rejected.
questions.more: Costs ballooned from seven million Australian dollars to 102 million and Utzon quit in 1966 after a row with the state government, leaving the country and never returning to see it finished in 1973. He solved the geometry of the roof by realising every shell could be cut from the same sphere.

questions.q: Fallingwater, the house Frank Lloyd Wright built over a waterfall in Pennsylvania, was designed for which family?
questions.w: The Kaufmanns, Pittsburgh department-store owners, who wanted a weekend house at Bear Run.
questions.more: Legend says Wright drew the whole design in the two hours it took Edgar Kaufmann to drive over after months of waiting. The cantilevered terraces sagged almost from the start, and steel supports were threaded in during a restoration in 2002.

questions.q: Which architect designed the glass pyramid in the courtyard of the Louvre?
questions.w: I. M. Pei, the Chinese-American architect chosen by President Mitterrand without a competition.
questions.more: Parisians were furious when it was unveiled in 1989 and one newspaper called it an annex to Disneyland. It has 673 glass panes, not the 666 that a persistent rumour claims. Pei also designed the Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong and lived to 102.

questions.q: Gothic cathedrals such as Notre-Dame stay up thanks to which external supports?
questions.w: Flying buttresses, stone arms that carry the outward push of the vaults down to piers outside the walls.
questions.more: Taking the load off the walls let builders open them up with huge stained-glass windows. Notre-Dame's were among the first, added around 1180 after cracks appeared. In the 2019 fire, the buttresses were what kept the weakened walls from folding inward.

questions.q: Which architect designed the titanium-clad Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, opened in 1997?
questions.w: Frank Gehry, whose swirling design was worked out with aircraft-industry software.
questions.more: The museum turned a rusting port city into a tourist destination so completely that planners talk about 'the Bilbao effect'. Its 33,000 titanium sheets are half a millimetre thick and ripple in the wind. Gehry's own house in Santa Monica is a modest bungalow wrapped in chain-link fencing.

questions.q: The Pantheon in Rome, finished around AD 126, still has the world's largest dome made of what unreinforced material?
questions.w: Concrete. The dome is 43 metres across and open to the sky through a nine-metre hole at the top.
questions.more: Roman builders lightened the mix as they went up, using heavy basalt at the base and porous pumice near the oculus. Rain falls through the hole onto a floor with hidden drains. The recipe for Roman concrete, which heals its own cracks with seawater, was only fully explained in 2023.

questions.q: Put these buildings in order of when they were completed, earliest first.
questions.w: Giza (about 2560 BC), the Parthenon (432 BC), Hagia Sophia (AD 537), Notre-Dame (largely finished by 1260).
questions.more: The Great Pyramid was the tallest structure on Earth for nearly 3,800 years. Hagia Sophia went up in under six years under the emperor Justinian and was a church, then a mosque, then a museum, and since 2020 a mosque again. Notre-Dame took the best part of a century.

questions.q: Which architect made 'less is more' the motto of modern architecture?
questions.w: Mies van der Rohe, last director of the Bauhaus and designer of the Seagram Building in New York.
questions.more: He borrowed the phrase from a Robert Browning poem. Mies fled Nazi Germany for Chicago in 1938, where his steel-and-glass towers set the template for the postwar office block. Robert Venturi answered him in 1966 with 'less is a bore'.

questions.q: Brutalism takes its name from the French term 'béton brut'. What does it mean?
questions.w: Raw concrete, left with the marks of its wooden formwork showing, as Le Corbusier used it after the war.
questions.more: The English critic Reyner Banham popularised 'Brutalism' in the 1950s and the style spread to council estates, universities and city halls worldwide. Boston City Hall and London's Barbican are landmarks of it. Long loathed, it now has fan clubs and a dedicated line of coffee-table books.

questions.q: Which Chicago building, finished in 1885, is generally counted as the world's first skyscraper?
questions.w: The Home Insurance Building, ten storeys tall, designed by William Le Baron Jenney.
questions.more: It was the first tall building carried by a metal skeleton rather than by its walls, which is what made real height possible. Jenney is said to have had the idea watching his wife set a heavy book on a birdcage. The building was demolished in 1931 to make way for a bigger one.

questions.q: Zaha Hadid, the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize in 2004, was born in which country?
questions.w: Iraq. She was born in Baghdad in 1950 and moved to London to study in 1972.
questions.more: For years she was called a 'paper architect' because her swooping designs were thought unbuildable; her first major building, a fire station in Germany, came when she was 43. The London Aquatics Centre, Beijing's Daxing airport and Baku's Heydar Aliyev Center are hers.

questions.q: Which of these were designed by Antoni Gaudí? Select all that apply.
questions.w: Casa Batlló, Park Güell and Casa Milà, all in Barcelona. The Guggenheim is Gehry's and the Alhambra is a medieval Moorish palace in Granada.
questions.more: Casa Milà, nicknamed La Pedrera, the stone quarry, has not a single straight wall. Park Güell was meant to be a gated housing estate for the rich; only two houses sold, and Gaudí lived in one of them. Seven of his works are together a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.q: Brasília, the purpose-built capital of Brazil inaugurated in 1960, was principally designed by which architect?
questions.w: Oscar Niemeyer designed the buildings; Lúcio Costa drew the aeroplane-shaped city plan.
questions.more: The city was built on empty savanna in 41 months on the promise of 'fifty years of progress in five'. Niemeyer, a lifelong communist, said his curves came from the mountains and women of Brazil. He kept working until he died in 2012, ten days short of his 105th birthday.
